newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: Ivorian cocoa in good shape despite weak rainfall.
newsitem.headline: Ivorian cocoa in good shape despite weak rainfall.

text.p: Ivorian cocoa areas had weak rains in early August and more is needed to confirm that a large developing 1997/98 crop (October-September) has escaped a possible El Nino drought, weather and crop analysts said on Monday.
Official national weather data for the first 10 days of August show rains averaged 16.6 mm at 10 monitored stations, against 20.8 mm in the previous 10 days and 16.7 mm before that.
Rains were concentrated in northern cocoa areas but crop analysts and upcountry buyers have since reported favourable sporadic rains in many other areas.
"So far so good. Nothing abnormal. We've had good light rains in many places," said one local crop analyst, adding that emerging crop forecasts would be firmed up in September.
If an El Nino weather pattern already hitting other parts of the world brought dry weather to Ivory Coast before October, harvest potential could be cut by up to 25 percent, he said.
One industry crop analyst told Reuters last week that the 1997/98 main crop could reach up to 1.1 million tonnes or at least equal the 1996/97 main crop -- which he put at 1.01 million tonnes.
Private reports have already been issued by other pod counters to clients.
Although it is not certain that El Nino will affect West Africa, the region's crop sizes have in the past sometimes been dented, one crop analyst said in July.
But he said a host of variables can mask the effect, particularly an expanding planted area or rising tree yields.
Cocoa farms remained in good shape in August, with adequate soil moisture levels despite drier than usual July weather, an analyst said this week after a tour of up-country producing areas.
Ivory Coast's small dry season (July-August) usually ends in late August.
Sporadic rains into September would dampen the effects of a late 1997 El Nino effect, even if it occurred, as main crop pods (April-September) would by then have developed, the analyst said.
Pods are harvested about five and a half months after developing. Small main crop pod fruits now appearing on trees could still be damaged by a drought before October.
Reduced bean sizes from any water shortage would also mean an overall harvest weight reduction even if pods survived.
Ivory Coast, the world's largest cocoa producer, rarely publishes crop data before the seasons close.
It notched up a record 1.2 million tonnes crop in 1995/96 after a better-than-expected 200,000 tonnes mid-crop.
The 1996/97 crop is set to total up to 1.15 million tonnes although some buyers expect cocoa to be stored for declaration in 1997/98 in the hope of a widely expected farmgate price rise.

The latest weather data, from Ivory Coast's national weather station, showed the following rainfall (mm) for the first 10 days of August in key growing areas plus the commercial capital Abidjan (previous 10 days bracketed).
Daloa 33.6 (8.9), Gagnoa 0.9 (6.3), San Pedro 0.9 (12.6), Tabou 8.9 (11.3), Man 113.8 (56.2), Dimbokro 0.1 (35.5), Yamoussoukro 5.5 (23.8), Abidjan 0.0 (8.4), Sassandra 0.5 (25.4), Adiake 1.5 (19.3).
